text.p: The following is a direct contribution from commodity statistician F.O. Licht in Ratzeburg, Germany. Please address any queries to Helmut Ahlfeld on +00 49 4541 88920.

Robusta futures in London continued to fall in a technical correction to recent sharp gains. However, roaster and trade purchases at the lows helped cushion the fall. March lost $58 to close at $1,540 per tonne, while May gave up $55 to close at $1,555 per tonne. Traders pegged the next key support for London's May contract at $1,500 per tonne. However, the future course of developments will be dictated by New York where profit taking accellerated causing the March and May contracts to plummet 9.75 cents/lb to 168.10 and 127.25 cents/lb respectively. Although the decline was mainly a technical retracement following last week's run-up to near two-year highs, the end of a state workers' strike in Colombia was also cited as a reason for the sharp fall. Moreover, a report from the former USDA attache indicated that the Brazilian crop recovered from frost was interpreted to mean the 1997/98 crop is not smaller, which, however, might not be the case. In spite of the sharp fall, fundamentals remain constructive

BRAZIL - Brazil's coffee trees have completely recovered from the damage caused by the twin frosts in 1994, consultant Leon Yalouz aid. Yalouz a former attache for the US Department of Agriculture (USDA) has recently returned from field trips, carried out to collect information for its revised crop estimate. Yalouz now works as an independent consultant as the USDA closed its Rio de Janeiro office in 1996, trade sources said. Yalouz indicated that he would like to publish his findings at the end of June.

BRAZIL - According to the National Coffee Council (CNC) coffee stocks held by Brazilian cooperatives totalled 2.63 million 60.5-kg bags on January 31, down from the 3.21 million bags held as of December 31, but up slightly from the 2.39 million bags held at the same stage in 1996. Sales by cooperatives reached 720,579 bags during January, showing that producers maintain their flow of coffee to the market, CNC said. Cooperatives received 146,822 bags of coffee during January, almost exactly twice the 72,370 bags delivered in January 1996, it added.

UNITED STATES - Supplies of green coffee housed in US warehouses rose in January 1997 by 15,000 bags to 1.342 million bags, the Green Coffee Association of New York said. In spite of the rise this is still significantly below the 2.151 million bags recorded at the end of January 1996.

DENMARK - Denmark imported 95,782 bags of coffee in October 1996, nearly 20 per cent more than was imported the same month the previous year. That brought total imports since the beginning of 1996 up to 838,500 bags, 19 per cent more than was imported the same period in 1995. Total imports in calendar year 1995 dropped by 14 per cent to 873,700 bags. Main suppliers of green coffee in January/October 1996 were Brazil (213,500 vs 269,200 bags) and Colombia (176,300 vs 145,300 bags). The country exported 81,900 bags of coffee in January/October 1996, 10 per cent more than was exported the same period in 1995. Total exports in calendar year 1995 dropped by 5.5 per cent to 91,200 bags.
